pattern: LinkedIn 'not X, it's Y' frame / generic editorializing
rule: no 'it's not X, it's Y'; opinions must be the author's, stated plainly
bad: What's actually useful here isn't the rendering - it's that the data is *already there*. You don't instrument anything, sign up for anything, or change how you launch Claude Code.
good: Because that transcript is written for every session automatically, you can inspect a run that already happened - even one you never intended to trace.
note: The take is generic and dressed in a thought-leadership frame. State the concrete capability instead.

pattern: vague fact where precision is available
rule: precision over smoothness; link primary sources
bad: Claude Code already writes a full transcript of every session to `~/.claude/projects/` as JSONL.
good: Claude Code already writes a full transcript of every session to `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-path>/<session-id>.jsonl`, containing the full conversation, tool calls, token usage, etc.
note: Make paths, versions, and numbers exact; add a schema/primary-source link where one exists.

pattern: describing an artifact instead of showing it
rule: show the artifact, don't describe it
bad: It only computes token-usage breakdowns by session, tool, project, and timeline - a cost lens rather than a conversation viewer.
good: It surfaces token-usage breakdowns by session, tool, project, and timeline, followed by the actual fenced cost table (Read at 56% of total cost, Task at $1.923/call, etc.).
note: Replace the description of output with the real output. A shown artifact beats any sentence about it.

rule: plain functional description over ranking
bad: **claude-code-trace** is the fullest example.
good: **claude-code-trace** is a Claude Code session log viewer with a GUI.
note: Say what a thing is and does, not where it ranks. Drop 'the X-est example' framings.

pattern: appeal to authority (quote a person's reaction as evidence)
rule: no appeal to authority; cite facts, not reactions
bad:
Simon Willison, writing about it, captured the appeal exactly [[4]]:
> "I've been thinking for a while it would be interesting to run some kind of HTTP proxy against the Claude Code CLI app to intercept its API traffic and take a peek at how it works."
He found the HTML interface "really nice," and used the tool to watch...
good: This is the level at which you can see the harness work: trace a session and you can watch the `dispatch_agent` tool spawn sub-agents that call other models, a pattern that burns through tokens fast [[4]].
note: Extract the concrete fact/mechanism, state it plainly, keep the [[n]] citation for verifiability. Drop the name-drop and the reaction quote. A quote is fine only when its exact wording is the point.

pattern: vendor marketing line quoted as evidence
rule: no appeal to authority; state the mechanism directly
bad:
Their framing [[11]]:
> "Most observability integrations only send data out, but agent development requires moving in both directions."
good: <cut the block quote; keep the [[11]] citation. The bidirectional point is already made in the author's own words in the next paragraph.>
note: A vendor's description of its own differentiator is not evidence. Say the mechanism yourself.

rule: no stacked short declaratives; fold into flowing prose; no colon-cliff list lead-ins
bad: This is the family that scales. It's the same instrumentation pattern you'd use for any production service, so it drops into infrastructure a platform team already runs. What it emits [[6]]:
good: Of the four families, this is the one that scales to a whole team. Because it relies on the same OpenTelemetry instrumentation you'd already point at a production service, a platform team doesn't have to stand up anything new - they can route Claude Code's telemetry into whatever monitoring stack they already run. That telemetry arrives as metrics, events, and the attributes attached to each [[6]]:
note: Clipped declaratives stacked for drumbeat read as a LinkedIn keynote. Join with because/so; replace 'What it emits:' with a real framing sentence.

rule: name the concrete subject as grammatical actor; give the reason with because/so
bad: The catch is content depth, and it's a deliberate one. Prompts are **redacted by default**...
good: Native OpenTelemetry deliberately trades away content depth. Prompts are **redacted by default**...
note: Don't label a point ('the catch', 'the tradeoff', 'the cost') before stating it. Subject then what it does then why, in one direct sentence.

pattern: sales-pitch framing of a tool's features
rule: plain functional description, not the vendor's voice
bad: The pitch beyond tracing is the rest of the ecosystem: prompt management, datasets, and evals, plus an Agent Skill / MCP server that lets Claude Code query its own production data from the terminal.
good: Tracing is just a small part of a larger Langfuse ecosystem: prompt management, datasets, and evals, plus an Agent Skill / MCP server that lets Claude Code query its own production data from the terminal, and that's where Langfuse's value lies.
note: 'The pitch is...' / 'The sell is...' put you in the vendor's voice. State it as your own assessment of the value.

pattern: meta-commentary (tell that an argument exists instead of making it)
rule: show, don't tell
bad: **Braintrust** [[11]] ships two plugins [[12]] and makes an explicit argument for why it's two.
good: **Braintrust** [[11]] ships two plugins [[12]], one for each direction the data flows.
note: Don't describe that a point is made; make it. Give the concrete reason (split by data direction).

rule: don't label a tool 'useful' above the artifact that already proves it
bad: It is a useful tool for monitoring cost and token usage:
good: It answers 'which tool is eating my budget?' in one command:
note: When the artifact (table/output) follows, frame what it reveals rather than labeling the tool 'useful'.

rule: no reflexive both-sidesing; commit to the take
bad: There is no single 'best' tool, just the 'right' tool for your needs.
good: <cut - the paragraph already states the real tradeoffs; this closer adds nothing and could end any comparison post.>
note: The canonical non-conclusion. Cut it; the surrounding prose already commits.
source: tracing-claude-code, Why the capture mechanism matters

pattern: filler adverb telling the reader how to feel
rule: cut 'surprisingly'/'interestingly' unless you say why
bad: The families sort surprisingly cleanly by what you're trying to do:
good: The families split by what you're trying to do:
note: If the cleanness is genuinely surprising, say why in a specific sentence. Otherwise drop the adverb.

rule: concrete over vague
bad: Adjacent tools blur the edges.
good: Two more tools don't fit cleanly into any family.
note: Replace the gesture with the concrete statement.

pattern: underdeveloped aside (named without link or expansion)
rule: if you name something, show what it does or cut it
bad: **Traceloop / OpenLLMetry** takes the OTEL-SDK route.
good: <add a link/citation and one concrete sentence on what it does, or cut the mention.>
note: Every other tool in the piece has a link and a concrete description; this half-thought doesn't earn its place as-is.

rule: connectives (also/too/as well/likewise) must have a real prior antecedent in the body, referring to a different thing
bad: The last family also uses hooks - Claude Code's lifecycle hooks fire scripts at defined points...
good: The last family works through hooks - Claude Code's lifecycle hooks fire scripts at defined points...
note: No earlier family was described as using hooks (the only prior mention is the TL;DR, describing this same family), so 'also' is a false back-reference.

rule: proofing
bad: Local viewers parses those logs into something readable on your machine.
good: Local viewers parse those logs into something readable on your machine.
note: 'viewers parse', not 'viewers parses'.

rule: proofing
bad: There are additional information that logs may not contain, such as system prompts and thinkig blocks.
good: Logs leave out some things - system prompts and thinking blocks.
note: 'information' is a mass noun ('there is', not 'there are'); 'thinkig' -> 'thinking'. Also re-voiced to avoid the awkward 'additional information that logs may not contain'.

pattern: content placed under a header it contradicts
rule: section placement — each paragraph must belong under its header
bad:
## Family 4: Eval platforms
...
Adjacent tools blur the edges. **Helicone** [[13]] sits in front of the LLM endpoint as a proxy - a fifth capture mechanism, really - and adds caching and cost reporting on top of logging.
good:
## Tools that don't fit the four families

A couple of general-purpose LLM-observability tools capture Claude Code's traffic without belonging to any of the four families above. **Helicone** [[13]] sits in front of the LLM endpoint as a proxy - a capture mechanism of its own - and adds caching and cost reporting on top of logging.
note: Helicone is a proxy, not an eval platform, yet was placed under the fourth family's header AND called 'a fifth capture mechanism' — placement contradicts category, and the uncounted ordinal compounds it. Promote orphan tools to their own section; state why they don't fit instead of the vague 'blur the edges'.
source: tracing-claude-code, Family 4 -> new 'Tools that don't fit' section

rule: the connective must match the author's actual stance; don't frame a strength as a drawback
bad: **Traceloop / OpenLLMetry** takes the OTEL-SDK route. Neither is Claude-Code-specific, but both will ingest its traffic.
good: **Traceloop / OpenLLMetry** takes the OTEL-SDK route. Because neither is tied to Claude Code, either can cover it alongside the rest of your LLM stack - one tool for everything, rather than a Claude-Code-specific one.
note: The 'but' frames 'not Claude-Code-specific' as a weakness redeemed by ingesting traffic, but being general-purpose is the actual advantage. Flip the concession into a 'because' that yields the benefit.

rule: delete fake-profound kickers; no announce-then-explain (make the concrete subject the actor)
bad: The families aren't mutually exclusive: many teams run an interceptor or local viewer for hands-on debugging *and* native OTEL for fleet cost tracking, because those answer genuinely different questions. The mistake is picking a tool before deciding which question you're asking - an eval platform won't show you the raw system prompt, and an interceptor won't tell you what the team spent last week.
good: In practice they stack. A team might run an interceptor or local viewer for hands-on debugging and native OTEL for fleet cost tracking, because each covers the other's blind spot: OTEL never shows you a raw system prompt, and an interceptor never tells you what the team spent last week.
note: Opens with the abstract label 'aren't mutually exclusive' before the concrete point, uses the filler intensifier 'genuinely different questions', and closes on the generic wisdom-kicker 'The mistake is picking a tool before deciding which question you're asking' — which just restates the intro. Keep the concrete payload (the tool pairing and the two blind-spot examples); cut the label, the intensifier, and the kicker; make the team the actor.
